claims.text: Progressive plastic deformation in FCC/BCC high-entropy-alloy multilayers under sustained loading is governed by interface-mediated dislocation activity.
Transformation twinning contributes to progressive plastic deformation in FCC/BCC high-entropy-alloy multilayers.
Nanoscale compositional heterogeneities at multilayer interfaces locally trigger transformation twinning.
Severe lattice distortions at multilayer interfaces locally trigger transformation twinning.
The starting coating contains distinct nanoscale FCC and BCC high-entropy-alloy phases with well-defined phase boundaries.
The starting coating combines high strength with some deformation tolerance.
Compositional gradients and lattice distortions at nanoscale multilayer interfaces concentrate stress.
Interface stress localization enhances dislocation emission.
Interface stress localization triggers transformation twinning.
A twin-bridging mechanism similar to the proposed multilayer mechanism has been observed in transformative high-entropy alloys.
Enhanced dislocation emission and transformation twinning facilitate progressive plastic deformation.
Sustained loading will increase dislocation density at multilayer interfaces relative to the as-deposited baseline.
Sustained loading will increase transformation-twin density at multilayer interfaces relative to the as-deposited baseline.
Interfacial dislocation and twin accumulation will produce localized softening or changes in strain rate.
Interfacial dislocation activity and transformation twinning will be more prominent in the HEA multilayers than in conventional metallic multilayers.
The proposed mechanism dominates only while the multilayer architecture remains nanoscale and intact.
The proposed mechanism dominates only when applied stress and temperature do not induce bulk phase transformations.
If stress or temperature crosses a threshold that induces extrinsic phase changes, a different deformation mechanism may govern.
